items.stem: Increasing the sample size makes the distribution of X̄…
items.markingKey: narrower (less spread). Variance σ²/n decreases.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the central limit theorem is useful when the population distribution is unknown.
items.answer: For large samples X̄ is approximately normal regardless of the population shape, so normal probabilities can be used for the sample mean.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: For large samples X̄ is approximately normal regardless of the population shape, so normal probabilities can be used for the sample mean. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "The central limit theorem says that a large sample is normally distributed." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It says the sample mean is approximately normally distributed; the individual data keep the population's shape.
items.markingKey: It says the sample mean is approximately normally distributed; the individual data keep the population's shape. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The masses of apples from an orchard have mean 165 g and standard deviation 24 g. (a) State the distribution of the mean X̄ of a random sample of 64, justifying your answer. (b) Find P(162.3 < X̄ < 167.7). (c) Find the smallest sample size for which P(|X̄ − 165| < 2.7) ≥ 0.9. (d) Explain what happens to the distribution of X̄ as n increases.
items.markingKey: (a) CLT, n large (R1); A1. (b) M1 A1. (c) 2.7/(σ/√n) ≥ 1.645 (M1) ⇒ n ≥ 213.8 (A1) ⇒ 214 (A1). (d) R1 the spread decreases (standard deviation σ/√n).

items.stem: Define the term "central limit theorem".
items.answer: For large n (usually n ≥ 30), the sample mean X̄ of n independent observations is approximately N(μ, σ²/n), whatever the population distribution
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: for large n (usually n ≥ 30), the sample mean X̄ of n independent observations is approximately N(μ, σ²/n), whatever the population distribution. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Denoted σ/√n, the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of X̄"?

items.stem: The daily step counts of office workers are known to be skewed, with mean 10700 steps and standard deviation 2400 steps. Explain why the mean of a random sample of 100 can be modelled by a normal distribution, and state its parameters.
items.markingKey: R1 by the central limit theorem, as n = 100 is large (≥ 30); R1 the shape of the population does not matter for large n; A1 mean 10700, variance σ²/n = 57600 (standard deviation 240).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the mean of a sample of 50 is less variable than a single observation.
items.answer: High and low values within the sample tend to balance out; the variance of the mean is σ²/50, much smaller than σ².
items.markingKey: Award marks for: High and low values within the sample tend to balance out; the variance of the mean is σ²/50, much smaller than σ². (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "A 95% confidence interval contains 95% of the data values." Explain the flaw in this statement.

items.stem: Explain why a t-interval is wider than a z-interval for the same data.
items.answer: The t-distribution has heavier tails to allow for the uncertainty in estimating σ by s, so its critical value is larger, especially for small samples.

items.stem: Explain the meaning of a 95% confidence interval for μ.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "standard error of the mean"?
options: For large n (usually n ≥ 30), the sample mean X̄ of n independent observations is approximately N(μ, σ²/n), whatever the population distribution
A test of H₀: ρ = 0 using the sample correlation r and n − 2 degrees of freedom
Denoted σ/√n, the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of X̄
Denoted s₀, the proportions (or probabilities) in each state at the start; after n steps the state is Tⁿs₀
items.answer: Denoted σ/√n, the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of X̄
items.markingKey: C. "standard error of the mean" is denoted σ/√n, the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of X̄.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A range of values, calculated from a sample, that contains the population parameter with a stated level of confidence"?
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of confidence interval.

items.stem: Sana writes: "After many steps the state vector is Tⁿ + s₀." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It is the matrix product Tⁿs₀.
items.markingKey: It is the matrix product Tⁿs₀. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The number of accidents per month at a junction has historically followed Po(3). After a change, 7 were observed in one period. Test at the 10% level whether the mean has increased. Ingrid uses P(X = 7) = 0.0216 as the p-value. Explain the error.
items.markingKey: R1 the p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme, P(X ≥ 7), not exactly 7; A1 0.0335; R1 conclusion reject H₀.

items.stem: The lengths of phone calls to a help line are known to be skewed, with mean 13 minutes and standard deviation 6 minutes. Explain why the mean of a random sample of 100 can be modelled by a normal distribution, and state its parameters.
items.markingKey: R1 by the central limit theorem, as n = 100 is large (≥ 30); R1 the shape of the population does not matter for large n; A1 mean 13, variance σ²/n = 0.360 (standard deviation 0.600).

items.stem: A 90% confidence interval for the mean of the daily step counts of office workers is (8188.9, 9556.5) steps. Rafael says: "There is a 90% probability that the true mean is in this interval, and 90% of individual values lie in it." Explain what is wrong.
items.markingKey: R1 μ is fixed; the 90% refers to the method: 90% of intervals constructed this way contain μ; R1 it is an interval for the mean, not for individual values (which are much more spread out, σ = 1440).

items.stem: For where an athlete trains each day, the transition matrix is T = [0.83, 0.19; 0.17, 0.81] (states gym, pool). Explain why the long-term proportions do not depend on the initial state, and find them.
items.markingKey: R1 all entries of T are positive (regular chain), so Tⁿ converges to a matrix with identical columns; R1 Tⁿs₀ → s for any s₀; A1 solve Ts = s with Σs = 1: 0.528, 0.472.

items.stem: The number of faults per 100 m of cable has historically followed Po(8). After a change, 10 were observed in one period. Test at the 10% level whether the mean has increased. Sofia uses P(X = 10) = 0.0993 as the p-value. Explain the error.
items.markingKey: R1 the p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme, P(X ≥ 10), not exactly 10; A1 0.283; R1 conclusion do not reject H₀.

items.stem: A random sample of the masses of apples from an orchard (g) gives: 161, 194, 191, 188, 265, 174, 136, 211, 179. (d) A supplier claims μ = 191.6; comment on this claim. (e) Using s as an estimate for σ, find the sample size needed for a 90% z-interval of width at most 11.1.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 A1. (b) R1 σ unknown, small sample, population assumed normal. (c) M1 A1 A1. (d) R1 191.6 lies inside the interval. (e) 2z*s/√n ≤ 11.1 (M1) ⇒ n = 113 (A1).

items.stem: A study follows 12000 players of an online game: the level each player is on after each game follows a Markov chain with T = [0.79, 0.56; 0.21, 0.44] (states level 1, level 2). Initially the proportions are (0.31, 0.69). (a) Explain what the entry in row 1, column 2 represents. (b) Find the expected number in each state after one period. (c) Find the proportions after three periods. (d) Find the steady-state vector. (e) Find the eigenvalues of T and explain the role of the eigenvalue 1.
items.markingKey: (a) R1 probability of moving from level 2 to level 1 in one period. (b) Ts₀ × 12000 (M1 A1). (c) T³s₀ (A1). (d) Ts = s (M1) A1. (e) A1; R1 the eigenvector for λ = 1 is the steady state; other eigenvalues have |λ| < 1, so their contributions die away.

items.stem: If X ~ N(μ, σ²), then X̄ for samples of size n is…
options: exactly N(μ, σ²/n) for any n
items.answer: exactly N(μ, σ²/n) for any n
items.markingKey: C. Means of normal variables are normal.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "t-interval"?
options: The distribution of a statistic (such as X̄) over all possible samples of a given size
Given by x̄ ± t*s/√n with n − 1 degrees of freedom, used when σ is unknown and estimated by the sample standard deviation
A sequence of states in which the probability of the next state depends only on the current state
Denoted s₀, the proportions (or probabilities) in each state at the start; after n steps the state is Tⁿs₀
items.answer: Given by x̄ ± t*s/√n with n − 1 degrees of freedom, used when σ is unknown and estimated by the sample standard deviation
items.markingKey: B. "t-interval" is given by x̄ ± t*s/√n with n − 1 degrees of freedom, used when σ is unknown and estimated by the sample standard deviation.

items.stem: For 12 randomly chosen cases, the correlation between screen time and hours of sleep is r = 0.893. Explain why a value of r this large may still not be significant, and what significance would show.
items.markingKey: R1 with a small sample a large r can arise by chance; R1 the test uses n − 2 = 10 degrees of freedom: p = 4.60 × 10⁻⁵; R1 significance shows evidence of linear correlation in the population, not causation.
